title: Why building eval platforms is hard — Phil Hetzel, Braintrust

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation platform design, eval maturity models, LLM judges, and the systems challenges of measuring agent quality. The talk addresses general-purpose eval platform architecture and developer-facing tooling for teams building AI agents. Coverage spans pre-production evaluation, deployment of agents, and production observability and monitoring. summary: Phil Hetzel of Braintrust opens with his background: 12 years in consulting at KPMG and Slalom Consulting, observing clients generating strong generative AI POCs that rarely reached production. He joined Braintrust after using it as a customer. Braintrust positions itself as an agent quality platform with two pillars: evals for pre-production experimentation and observability for production monitoring. Hetzel explains why evals matter: LLMs have extreme variability, agents are becoming the expected customer interaction mode, and untested agents create risk across brand, compliance, cost, and maintenance dimensions. He normalizes starting with spreadsheets but notes a basic eval setup needs three things: agent execution, a UI for outputs and scores, and input examples. The full complexity includes making evals a multi-persona problem involving product engineers, AI engineers, systems engineers, and domain SMEs. Hetzel outlines progressive maturity stages: Stage 1 spreadsheets are accessible but amount to documentation rather than experimentation. Stage 2 vibe-coded custom UIs bring more people in but still function as reporting. Stage 3 introduces true experimentation with sandboxes for tweaking agent parameters and comparing configurations. Beyond Stage 3, Hetzel connects observability and evals as the same systems problem via a flywheel: observe production behavior, pull real examples back into offline evals, iterate, and repeat for the agent's lifetime. This widens scope to become a tracing and logging platform. Agent traces are nasty: semi-structured, unstructured, very large (spans of 10-20MB), high velocity, with diverse read patterns requiring both low-latency and aggregate query support. Braintrust's old approach used an open-source data warehouse, a custom DSL called BTQL, and DuckDB in-browser, but struggled with full-text search across traces. Hetzel emphasizes this is fundamentally a systems problem, not just UI/UX. He notes headless use cases where coding agents interact with eval platforms directly, the need to surface unknown unknowns through topic modeling, building for agents not just humans, and non-functional requirements like RBAC and data masking. In Q&A, he explains multimodal inputs and outputs are stored in object storage and displayed directly in traces.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Hetzel introduces himself, his background in consulting at KPMG and Slalom Consulting, and his current role leading solutions engineering at Braintrust. He explains he joined after using the platform as a customer to help POCs reach production.

sections.title: Braintrust Overview
sections.summary: Brief positioning of Braintrust as an agent quality platform with two pillars: evals for pre-production experimentation and observability for production monitoring. Hetzel notes this is not a sales pitch.

sections.title: Why Evals Are Important
sections.summary: Evals matter because LLMs have extreme variability and agents are becoming the norm for customer interactions. Without evals, organizations risk brand, compliance, cost, and maintenance problems.

sections.title: The Tip of the Iceberg: Basic Eval Components
sections.summary: Hetzel normalizes starting with spreadsheets and identifies three basic eval components: agent execution, UI for outputs and scores, and input examples. He emphasizes this is only the visible part of a much larger problem.

sections.title: Why Eval Platforms Are Complicated
sections.summary: The complexity comes from the underlying LLM technology, the multi-persona nature of the problem involving engineers and SMEs, and the fact that evals themselves become a systems problem.

sections.title: Stage 1: Spreadsheet-Based Evals
sections.summary: Spreadsheets are a valid starting point with no barrier to entry, but they amount to documentation rather than experimentation, are hard to compare across runs, lack analytics, exclude non-technical users, and are slow.

sections.title: Stage 2: Vibe-Coded Custom UIs
sections.summary: Engineers vibe-code bespoke UIs with better databases, bringing more people into the fold. However, this still functions as reporting rather than encouraging true iteration and experimentation.

sections.title: Stage 3: Experimentation Platforms
sections.summary: True experimentation allows both technical and non-technical users to tweak agent parameters in sandboxes, compare configurations, and see bubbled-up scores. Hetzel shows a UI example for non-technical experimentation.

sections.title: The Flywheel: Connecting Observability and Evals
sections.summary: Hetzel explains that observability and evals are the same systems problem. He shares how Braintrust evolved from evals-only to adding observability after discovering a customer piping production traffic into evals. The flywheel loop: observe production behavior, pull real examples into offline evals, iterate, and repeat for the agent's lifetime.

sections.title: Widening Scope and Online Evals
sections.summary: Building the flywheel widens scope to include tracing and logging. Benefits include higher signal from real user interactions and the ability to perform online evals with alerting on observability traffic.

sections.title: The Build-It-You-Own-It Problem
sections.summary: If you vibe-code your own platform, you own it and must maintain it at industry pace. Braintrust's bet is that solving this ongoing challenge is their business.

sections.title: Agent Trace Complexity
sections.summary: Agent traces are nasty: semi-structured, unstructured, text-heavy, very large, numerous, and high velocity. Cramming a 1GB trace into a Postgres row causes performance problems. Traditional data warehouse technologies struggle with full-text search across traces.

sections.title: Braintrust's Old Data Architecture
sections.summary: Their old approach used two query layers: low-latency ingestion for instant trace viewing and an open-source data warehouse for aggregate analysis, stitched with a custom DSL called BTQL and DuckDB in-browser. This failed for customers like Notion needing full-text search across traces.

sections.title: Evals as a Systems Problem
sections.summary: Measuring agent quality is a systems problem, not just UI/UX. Agent traces are large (10-20MB spans vs traditional kilobytes), unstructured, high velocity, with diverse read patterns. The right data platform is needed for functional requirements like full-text search and headless coding agent use cases.

sections.title: Future Considerations and Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Future eval platform needs include surfacing unknown unknowns via topic modeling, building for agents as users not just humans, non-functional requirements like RBAC and data masking, and automatic tracing through AI proxies or gateways.

sections.title: Q&A: Multimodal Inputs and Prompt Management
sections.summary: Hetzel explains multimodal inputs and outputs are stored in object storage, referenced, and displayed directly in traces. Prompt management can be in Braintrust but does not have to be.
